newsitem.title: UK: Breakdown of major nations' offer of Zaire help.
newsitem.headline: Breakdown of major nations' offer of Zaire help.

text.p: Plans for a large intervention force in eastern Zaire remained on hold on Thursday as an estimated 100,000 Hutu refugees took to the road again, possibly signalling another mass exodus to their homeland.

Meanwhile the United Nations sent an assessment team into Zaire's Bukavu and said it had located -- for the first time in weeks -- up to 700,000 missing Rwandan refugees with satellite pictures and overflights.
The missing refugees are central to the debate over military intervention.
Three meetings are due to be held this week to reassess the refugee situation. Politicians were due to meet in New York on Thursday to decide what help the refugees now need.

Military officials from nations expected to contribute to the multinational force -- including France, the United States, Britain and Canada -- have scheduled a meeting for 1000 GMT on Friday in Stuttgart, Germany.
The meeting, which has been delayed since Wednesday, will be chaired by Canada and will review the general scope of the mission needed since the refugees began returning home.
Western aid chiefs, donor countries and relief agencies will gather in Geneva on Saturday to coordinate aid plans for the refugees, with their action now expected to be largely based in Rwanda.

CANADA -- said on Wednesday that most nations involved in the humanitarian crisis in Africa believed a military force was still needed to deliver aid. Canadian Deputy Foreign Minister Gordon Smith said that military planners needed to develop a range of options. The options, he said, ranged from convoys and air support that might not require ground troops to a scaled-down version of the original intervention plan that envisaged at least 10,000 soldiers in the region.

FRANCE -- says multinational intervention is still needed to help refugees in Zaire, despite the sudden return of a large number of them to Rwanda. The French Foreign Ministry said there were still 300,000 refugees in Bukavu, 200,000 near Goma and another 200,000 in Uvira and that it was necessary to ensure the security of relief convoys to prevent humanitarian disaster.

BRITAIN -- plans to send a photo-reconnaissance plane over east Zaire on Friday to assess the refugee crisis. The government said Britain remained prepared to take part in the multinational military force, but along with other Western nations it needed more information before it could decide how to provide help.

UNITED STATES -- Washington indicated it had cancelled plans to send combat troops to Zaire and was preparing instead for a military air relief operation. U.S. officials say fewer than 1,000 logistical personnel were now needed for a military operation led by Canada in Rwanda. Under the new plan about 200 U.S. air Force personnel would be sent to Kigali airport in Rwanda, 500 to Entebbe in Uganda and about 100 to Mombasa in Kenya to prepare for the air relief operation. President Bill Clinton said no final decision on this had been made.

SPAIN -- says that a multinational force was still needed to mount a humanitarian mission to Zaire. Spain, which along with France led calls for international military intervention, said it was still preparing to send a force but that its task would have to be redefined after the refugee exodus back to Rwanda.

SOUTH AFRICA -- President Nelson Mandela has pledged to contribute troops to a multinational peace force on condition it has a regional leader from the Great Lakes region. South Africa has not said what form their contribution would take.

BELGIUM - Zaire's former colonial ruler has said it was ready to send soldiers to Africa to train local troops for an eventual U.N. peacekeeping force in east Zaire, but says it will not take part directly in a force in Zaire, Rwanda or Burundi.

GERMANY - has ruled out sending German troops to Zaire, but the government said it would release an extra 10 million marks for humanitarian organisations to help cope with the flood of Rwandan refugees heading home from Zaire such as projects to ensure they had clean drinking water.

THE NETHERLANDS -- says an international force to mount a humanitarian operation in Zaire should also be mandated to repatriate the refugees and disarm the Hutu militia. Officials have suggested the Dutch might decline to take part in the operation if its conditions for the mandate were not met. They say 270 members of the Dutch Air Mobile Brigade are preparing.

IRELAND -- has said it will provide troops for the proposed force if asked. It is expected to contribute a specialist unit of soldiers such as engineers, military police or logistics personnel. Officials say it is unlikely to exceed 100 soldiers.
FINLAND -- says it will not send troops but is studying other ways it can help.
